content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In prophetic and apocalyptic interpretation, the moon most commonly functions as part of the divinely ordered cosmos; its darkening, turning to blood, or otherwise failing symbolizes the Day of the Lord, divine judgment, and the upheaval of the present world order.","primary_basis":["Isaiah 13:9–10 — the moon withholds its light during the day of the Lord against Babylon.","Isaiah 24:21–23 — the moon is confounded when the Lord reigns in judgment.","Joel 2:10, 2:30–31; 3:15 — the moon darkens or turns to blood before the day of the Lord.","Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24; Luke 21:25 — the moon is darkened amid signs accompanying eschatological upheaval.","Acts 2:19–20 — Joel’s blood-red moon imagery is applied to the coming day of the Lord.","Revelation 6:12–17 — the moon becomes like blood at the opening of the sixth seal."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The moon represents the Church, which has no light of its own but reflects the light of Christ, as the moon reflects the sun.","basis":["Genesis 1:16 — the lesser light is allegorically associated with a subordinate, reflected luminary.","Psalm 19:1–6 — celestial light imagery is sometimes incorporated into Christ-and-Church allegory.","Song of Songs 6:10 — the woman 'fair as the moon' has traditionally been interpreted ecclesiologically or Marianly.","Revelation 12:1 — the woman clothed with the sun and associated with the moon is often read as the Church, Israel, Mary, or a combination of these."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The moon represents a mother, matriarch, or feminine figure.","basis":["Genesis 37:9–10 — Jacob interprets Joseph’s sun, moon, and stars as father, mother, and brothers.","Revelation 12:1 — the moon appears beneath the feet of the symbolic woman, encouraging feminine, Marian, Israelite, and ecclesial readings."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The moon symbolizes Israel or the covenant people, especially in interpretations of Joseph’s dream and the woman of Revelation 12.","basis":["Genesis 37:9–10 — the celestial family is associated with the patriarchal household that becomes Israel.","Revelation 12:1–6 — the woman’s twelve-star and messianic imagery is commonly connected with Israel, though the moon’s specific meaning remains disputed."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The moon signifies appointed times, seasons, liturgical order, and the stability of God’s created or covenantal order.","basis":["Genesis 1:14–18 — the heavenly lights mark signs, seasons, days, and years.","Psalm 104:19 — God appoints the moon for seasons.","Psalm 89:35–37 — the moon is an enduring witness to the promised permanence of David’s line.","Jeremiah 31:35–36 — the fixed order of sun, moon, and stars supports the endurance of Israel before God."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The moon symbolizes mutability, transience, or the changing character of earthly things, in contrast with God’s constancy.","basis":["Psalm 72:5–7; 89:36–37 — comparisons with the moon can suggest duration while also inviting reflection on created changeability.","Isaiah 60:19–20; Revelation 21:23 — the redeemed city’s lack of need for sun or moon has traditionally supported contrasts between created, changeable light and God’s unchanging glory."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is no settled, universal Christian symbolic definition of the moon. Its meaning is strongly context-dependent. Judgment and cosmic upheaval are the clearest recurring meanings when the moon is altered in prophetic texts; reflected light and the Church are prominent in traditional allegory but are not explicitly defined as such by Scripture. In narrative passages such as Genesis 37, the text itself supplies a different, family-specific interpretation."}
